title: Container security basics
idea: Container security is least privilege: give a container only the access it needs, so a flaw in your app does less damage.
points: A container process runs as `root`, the all-powerful account, unless the image says otherwise.
Official Node images ship a `node` user; `USER node` switches to it.
Files you `COPY` and values you set with `ENV` stay readable inside the image.
Drop what the app does not need: capabilities, write access, new privileges.

parts.label: Command
parts.note: Starts the Book Store API in the background as a container named `api`.

parts.label: Read-only filesystem
parts.note: Makes the root filesystem read-only. Add `--tmpfs /tmp` if the app needs scratch space.

parts.label: Capabilities
parts.note: Drops every Linux capability, the separate privileges that make up root's power. Add back only what you need.

parts.label: No new privileges
parts.note: Stops processes in the container from gaining extra privileges after they start.

parts.label: Loopback only
parts.note: Publishes the port on the host's `127.0.0.1` only. Without it, the port listens on all host addresses.

parts.label: Image
parts.note: The image to run. Its Dockerfile sets `USER node`, so the process does not run as `root`.

code.caption: The chapter's Dockerfile with one new line: the app runs as `node`.

walk.text: Dependencies install as `root`, before the user switch. That is fine at build time.
Copied files belong to `root`, so `node` can read the code but cannot rewrite it.
From here on, `RUN` steps and the container's process use `node`, not `root`.

code.caption: Pass secrets when the container starts, then check what the process can do.

walk.text: Read secrets from a local `.env` file at start; keep that file out of the image.
Print the user the container's process runs as.
Try to create a file in `/app`. It fails: `root` owns that folder.

pitfalls: A `COPY . .` also copies `.env` into the image; list it in `.dockerignore`.
Never share `/var/run/docker.sock`, Docker's control socket, with a container; it can then control Docker.
Skip `--privileged`: it grants every capability and all host devices.

quiz.q: An image copied `.env`, then a later line ran `RUN rm .env`. Is the secret gone?
options: Yes, the file no longer exists
No, the earlier layer still contains it
Yes, but only after a restart
No, but only on public registries
quiz.why: Image layers are read-only. `RUN rm` adds a new layer that hides the file, but the earlier layer still holds it.

takeaway: Run as non-root, keep secrets out of images, drop privileges you do not need.
